title: After Endgame, Primary Documents must change as slowly and as little as possible while staying adapted
content:
A.1.2.2.1.2 gives Primary Documents two distinct regimes. In the transition to Endgame they "can be modified with no restrictions, using the governance processes specified elsewhere in the Atlas." Once the Endgame State is reached, they "generally must be modified as slowly as possible, and as little as possible while remaining fully adapted to the external environment."

This creates a third mutability class between fixed and free. Immutable Documents stop changing entirely at Endgame (A.1.2.2.1.1); Primary Documents keep changing but under a standing burden of justification. The qualifier "while remaining fully adapted to the external environment" is what keeps it from becoming de facto immutability — a Primary Document that has fallen out of step with reality must be changed, and slowness is not an excuse for staleness.

The reasoning is a direct application of the drift thesis. Every amendment is an opportunity for slippery slope misalignment, so amendment frequency is itself a risk variable. Minimizing edits minimizes exposure, but only up to the point where non-adaptation becomes the larger risk.

The unresolved part is who arbitrates that trade-off. "As little as possible while remaining fully adapted" states an optimum without specifying a measure, so in practice the judgment falls to whoever holds interpretive authority — which is why the same Scope invests so heavily in facilitator caution duties and documented precedent.
description: A.1.2.2.1.2 replaces unrestricted modification with a minimum-change duty at Endgame — a standing bias against churn that is not the same as immutability.
